newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel marks Rabin murder, fears guerrilla raids.
newsitem.headline: Israel marks Rabin murder, fears guerrilla raids.

text.p: Israel marked a year since the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin by sealing off the West Bank and Gaza Strip on Thursday in fear of Palestinian guerrilla attacks.

The peace that was to be Rabin's legacy remained elusive as Israeli and Palestinian negotiators ended another round of talks on Wednesday without coming to terms on a promised Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron.

"There will be a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip starting at midnight (2200 GMT on Wednesday) due to the vast warning of intentions of suicide attacks the next few days," said an Israeli army spokesman.

Officials said the Jewish state had gone on high security alert ahead of the anniversary of the assassination of Fathi Shqaqi, the leader of the militant Islamic Jihad group behind suicide attacks in Israel.
Shqaqi was gunned down in Malta on October 26 last year in what Palestinians believe was an attack by Israel's Mossad secret service. The militant group has vowed to avenge his murder.
Nowhere was the tension between Arabs and Jews as high as in Hebron, the religiously charged town that is home to 400 Jewish settlers who live among 100,000 Palestinians.
"We in Hebron are preparing many arms so that we will have weapons against the settlers," a Palestinian resident in Hebron told Israel Radio on Wednesday.
"We are preparing a big surprise. We have a lot of arms here, more than 800 pieces. They want to make trouble, we'll make trouble for them."
Armed Jewish settlers tried to lay claim to Arab-owned shops in the centre of the West Bank town on Wednesday but were stopped by Israeli police who made one arrest.
Israel was to hand over parts of Hebron to the Palestinians under a deal Rabin's government reached with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat more than a year ago.

Israel implemented part of the agreement, withdrawing troops from other major towns in the West Bank to make room for Palestinian self-rule but delaying the Hebron redeployment after a spree of suicide bombings in February and March.
The general election victory in May of Israeli hardliner Benjamin Netanyahu, long opposed to the peace deals with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), further clouded the Hebron withdrawal.
"I am sorry to say that the gap (between negotiators)...is still very wide," Arafat told a news conference in the West Bank on Wednesday.
In an interview Israel Television broadcast to mark the anniversary of Rabin's assassination, Arafat said he warned the Israeli leader weeks before he was murdered to watch out for extremists.
Yigal Amir, a religious Jew who viewed Rabin as a traitor for his peace deals with the PLO, gunned him down at a Tel Aviv peace rally on November 4 after stalking him for months.
"I don't remember much from those days...it's been one long nightmare since then," said Rabin's granddaughter Noa Ben-Artzi, whose eulogy moved world leaders to tears at Rabin's funeral.

"Everything that happened after the murder, if it was strange or ugly or painful, it doesn't resemble the things that happened before. My world is divided into two and if you ask me, it's clear that I would like to live in the old one," she told Israel Radio.
In Tel Aviv, hundreds of Israeli youths marched with torches from the site where Rabin was shot to the hospital where he died.
Rabin's family was expected to hold a memorial ceremony at his grave in Jerusalem on Thursday, the anniversary of the murder according to the Jewish calendar.
In schools, teachers were due to spend an hour in the morning talking to students about Rabin and the events that led to his assassination.
